questions.question: Which synovial fluid white blood cell (WBC) count is considered 92% specific for a diagnosis of septic arthritis?
questions.detail: A fluid WBC count of >50,000 is highly specific (92%) for septic arthritis, although it is only seen in 62% of cases. A count of >100,000 is 99% specific but has very low sensitivity.

questions.question: What is the most common route of spread for osteomyelitis in the pediatric population?
choices: Contiguous spread from a soft tissue ulcer
Direct inoculation from a puncture wound
questions.detail: In children, hematogenous spread is the most common route of infection, typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus. In adults, contiguous spread or direct inoculation is more common.

questions.question: In the pathology of chronic osteomyelitis, what is the term for a piece of necrotic bone that has become separated from viable bone?
questions.detail: A sequestrum is necrotic bone separated from viable bone by granulation tissue; it can harbor living organisms and act as a nidus for recurrent infection.

questions.question: Why can hematogenous osteomyelitis in infants (up to 12 months old) involve the epiphysis and the adjacent joint?
choices: The physis is not yet formed.
Bridging vessels cross the physis in this age group.
The periosteum is more tightly adherent than in adults.
Infants lack a central medullary cavity.
The Batson plexus is more prominent in infancy.
questions.detail: In infants, vessels bridge the physis, allowing metaphyseal infection to spread into the epiphysis and joint. In older children, these capillaries do not cross the physis.

questions.question: Which imaging finding is a key feature distinguishing diabetic foot osteomyelitis from Charcot (neuropathic) arthropathy on MRI?
choices: Bone marrow edema on STIR sequences
Presence of a cutaneous ulcer and a sinus tract to the bone
Enhancement of the marrow on post-gadolinium T1 images
Low T1 marrow signal in a reticular pattern
questions.detail: Diabetic foot osteomyelitis is almost always associated with a cutaneous ulcer and sinus tract, and the cortex is often disrupted. Charcot joints typically have an intact cortex and no associated ulcer/sinus tract.

questions.question: A 'Brodie abscess' is a characteristic radiographic lesion of which phase of osteomyelitis?
questions.detail: A Brodie abscess is a hallmark of subacute osteomyelitis, consisting of a walled-off intra-osseous abscess with central lucency and peripheral sclerosis.

questions.question: Osteomyelitis caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa is classically associated with which clinical scenario?
choices: IV drug use with spinal involvement
questions.detail: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the classic organism responsible for osteomyelitis following a puncture wound to the foot through a sneaker.

questions.question: In adult vertebral osteomyelitis, where does the infection typically begin?
choices: In the subendplate region of the vertebral body
At the attachment of the ligamentum flavum
questions.detail: In adults, infection typically begins in the subendplate region and then spreads to the disc and adjacent body. In children, isolated discitis can occur because the disc is still directly vascularized.

questions.question: On a three-phase Tc-99m MDP bone scan, how is acute osteomyelitis distinguished from cellulitis?
choices: Cellulitis is negative on all three phases.
Osteomyelitis is only positive on the delayed phase.
Osteomyelitis is positive on all three phases, while cellulitis is negative on the delayed phase.
Cellulitis is only positive on the delayed phase.
Both are positive on all three phases, but osteomyelitis is more intense.
questions.detail: Acute osteomyelitis shows increased uptake on the flow, blood pool, and delayed phases. Cellulitis shows increased flow and blood pool activity but is negative on delayed images.

questions.question: What is the MRI hallmark for the reliable diagnosis of osteomyelitis in the marrow?
choices: Confluent intramedullary low T1 signal (darker than muscle)
High T2 signal that does not involve the cortex
Preserved fatty marrow signal on all sequences
questions.detail: Confluent intramedullary signal change (low T1/high T2) is strongly associated with osteomyelitis. Hazy reticular or subcortical patterns are generally not associated with infection.

questions.question: Which aggressive soft-tissue infection is a surgical emergency characterized by gas bubbles in the tissues on CT?
questions.detail: Necrotizing fasciitis is an aggressive infection (often Clostridium) requiring immediate debridement; the characteristic finding is gas within the soft tissues.

questions.question: The 'Wimberger sign' (deep erosion of the medial proximal tibial metaphysis) is a classic finding in which infection?
questions.detail: The Wimberger sign refers to destructive erosion of the medial proximal tibial metaphysis in congenital syphilis.

questions.question: Which condition is an inflammatory, nonpyogenic disorder of the bone that can mimic pyogenic osteomyelitis but lacks abscesses or sequestra?
questions.detail: CRMO is a nonpyogenic inflammatory disorder characterized by migratory lytic/sclerotic lesions; it does not feature abscesses, sequestra, or fistulae.

questions.question: What is the clinical significance of a chronic drainage sinus tract in the setting of chronic osteomyelitis?
choices: It indicates the infection has been successfully cleared.
It predisposes the patient to squamous cell carcinoma.
It is pathognomonic for Salmonella infection.
It prevents the development of an involucrum.
It is the primary site for Brodie abscess formation.
questions.detail: Chronic drainage from a sinus tract in long-standing osteomyelitis predisposes the patient to the development of squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.question: In a child presenting with a hip effusion and limp, what is the most common organism responsible if the diagnosis is septic arthritis?
questions.detail: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of hematogenous osteomyelitis and secondary septic arthritis in children.
